sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: To describe initial vascular access among incident haemodialysis patients, identify patient-level factors associated with starting haemodialysis with an arteriovenous fistula (AVF) rather than a central venous catheter (CVC), and explore clinical and biochemical status after 3 months.

sec.title: Design
sec.p: Multicentre retrospective observational study.

sec.title: Setting
sec.p: Dialysis centres in six tertiary hospitals in Taizhou, southeastern Zhejiang, China, from 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2023.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Of 1227 database records assessed, 6 were excluded (5 initial arteriovenous graft records and 1 record outside the prespecified study period), leaving 1221 incident haemodialysis patients.

sec.title: Primary and secondary outcome measures
sec.p: The primary outcome was initial AVF rather than CVC use. Secondary exploratory outcomes were mean arterial pressure and biochemical measurements after 3 months; dialysis adequacy, access patency, access infection and mortality were unavailable.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Initial access was an AVF in 446/1,221 patients (36.5%) and a CVC in 775/1221 (63.5%); CVCs comprised 413 tunnelled cuffed and 362 non-tunnelled catheters. Initial AVF use varied across hospitals from 18.9% to 49.0%. In a centre-adjusted model using 20 multiply imputed datasets, higher baseline haemoglobin (adjusted OR per 10 g/L 1.144, 95% CI 1.060 to 1.234), albumin (per 5 g/L 1.411, 95% CI 1.242 to 1.603) and calcium (per 0.1 mmol/L 1.112, 95% CI 1.052 to 1.176) and lower C-reactive protein (per doubling 0.845, 95% CI 0.797 to 0.896) were associated with initial AVF use. At 3 months, no AVF-CVC difference remained robust after baseline and centre adjustment and false-discovery-rate control.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Initial AVF use was uncommon and was associated with baseline clinical status and centre. These observational findings support timely predialysis assessment and individualised vascular-access planning, but they do not show that access type caused subsequent biochemical differences.

caption.title: STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY

list-item.p: This multicentre study included incident haemodialysis patients from six tertiary hospitals over five calendar years and describes regional variation in initial vascular access.
Reanalysis of the participant-level database corrected cohort counts, reported variable-specific denominators and added a participant flow diagram.
The main model used multiple imputation and centre fixed effects; a complete-case analysis assessed sensitivity to missing covariates.
The 3-month analyses were reframed as exploratory clinical and biochemical associations, adjusted for baseline values and centre, and interpreted after false-discovery-rate control.

Retrospective measurement, residual confounding, incomplete timing and operational detail for the database-recorded centre classification, and absence of dialysis adequacy, access patency, access-related infection and mortality data limit interpretation and generalisability.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is an important contributor to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. In China, the estimated prevalence of CKD among adults is 8.2%.1 Haemodialysis is a major kidney-replacement therapy for people with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD), and reliable vascular access is essential.2 3 Arteriovenous fistulas (AVFs) and central venous catheters (CVCs) are commonly used at dialysis initiation. CVCs permit immediate treatment but are associated with infection, thrombosis and central venous stenosis, whereas AVFs generally have fewer access-related complications.4–9 However, associations between access type and clinical outcomes are strongly affected by patient selection, illness severity and predialysis care.

Contemporary guidance no longer treats a single access hierarchy as appropriate for every patient. The 2019 Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative guideline places vascular access within an individualised ESKD Life-Plan that considers prognosis, urgency, anatomy and patient preferences.10 Regional data on access used at first haemodialysis remain limited in China. We therefore described initial access in six Taizhou hospitals, evaluated patient-level factors associated with initial AVF use and explored 3-month clinical and biochemical status without assigning causality to access type.

sec.title: Study design, setting and participants
sec.p: We conducted a multicentre retrospective observational study of patients who initiated maintenance haemodialysis between 1 January 2019 and 31 December 2023 at Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, Enze Hospital, Taizhou Central Hospital, Xianju People’s Hospital, Yuhuan People’s Hospital and Tiantai People’s Hospital, all in Taizhou, Zhejiang, China. All six participating hospitals authorised the collection and use of routinely collected data for this study. Eligible patients had ESKD, received haemodialysis for the first time and were expected to require maintenance treatment. Records for acute kidney injury or drug intoxication were ineligible. For the present AVF-CVC comparison, records with an initial arteriovenous graft were excluded.

sec.title: Data source, variables and definitions
sec.p: Data were extracted from the Heal Haemodialysis Information System and the consolidated study database. Variables included age, sex, education, insurance, primary kidney disease, hospital, initial vascular access, catheter subtype, blood pressure and laboratory measurements. Baseline measurements were those recorded within 1 week before haemodialysis initiation; the database did not retain the exact timing of C-reactive protein (CRP) sampling relative to catheter insertion. Follow-up measurements were those designated as 3-month values in the database. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) was calculated as (systolic blood pressure+2×diastolic blood pressure)/3.

Initial access was classified as AVF or CVC. The CVC group included tunnelled cuffed catheters (often used for intermediate-term or longer-term access) and non-tunnelled catheters (generally used temporarily). Because access changes, patency, infection and catheter removal dates were not recorded, we did not classify CVCs as uniformly ‘semi-permanent’ or relate inflammation to access patency.

The source database placed Taizhou Hospital and Enze Hospital in a centre-level category denoting specialised vascular-access physicians. The investigators clarified that the other four centres subsequently developed vascular-access teams; however, the database did not capture when these teams were established or standardised details of staffing, training, referral pathways, procedural volume and service availability. We therefore retained the recorded grouping only as a centre-level descriptive classification. It should not be interpreted as a stable with-versus-without-team exposure throughout 2019–2023 and was not entered together with hospital fixed effects in the patient-level model.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary outcome was use of an AVF rather than a CVC at the first haemodialysis treatment. Exploratory 3-month outcomes were MAP, haemoglobin, albumin, serum calcium, serum phosphorus, parathyroid hormone (PTH) and CRP. We refer to these as clinical and biochemical status rather than dialysis quality because standard adequacy measures such as Kt/V and urea reduction ratio were not available.

sec.title: Data quality and missing data
sec.p: We checked duplicate identifiers, internal consistency and prespecified physiologically plausible ranges. Values outside those ranges and non-numerical entries were set to missing and retained in an audit log. CRP values reported below a detection limit were represented by one-half of that limit. Variable-specific denominators are reported. The primary multivariable analysis used multiple imputation for missing covariates, and complete-case analysis was used as a sensitivity analysis. 3-month models used available cases for each outcome.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Continuous variables were summarised as median (IQR) because several distributions were skewed and were compared descriptively using the Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables were summarised as n (%) and compared using Pearson’s χ² test. The prespecified patient-level logistic regression outcome was initial AVF use. Covariates were age, sex, insurance, education, diabetic nephropathy, baseline MAP, haemoglobin, albumin, calcium and log2-transformed CRP; hospital fixed effects accounted for centre-level differences. Haemoglobin, albumin and calcium were scaled to clinically interpretable units. Missing covariates were imputed in 20 datasets using iterative chained equations with posterior sampling, and estimates were combined using Rubin’s rules. A complete-case model assessed sensitivity. Variance inflation factors were inspected. Model discrimination and calibration were described in the complete-case dataset using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve with bootstrap CIs and the Hosmer-Lemeshow test. Exploratory 3-month linear models adjusted for the corresponding baseline value, age, sex, diabetic nephropathy and hospital, used heteroscedasticity-consistent SEs and applied Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate control across seven outcomes. P values were two-sided. Analyses were performed in Python V.3.12 using pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn and statsmodels.

sec.title: Patient and public involvement
sec.p: Patients and the public were not involved in the design, conduct, reporting or dissemination plans of this retrospective study.

sec.title: General characteristics
sec.p: Of 1227 records assessed, five arteriovenous graft records and one record dated outside 2019–2023 were excluded, leaving 1221 patients (figure 1). Initial access was an AVF in 446 (36.5%) and a CVC in 775 (63.5%); 792 (64.9%) patients were male. Baseline characteristics and variable-specific denominators are shown in table 1.

sec.title: Vascular access profile
sec.p: Patients who initiated with an AVF had higher baseline haemoglobin, albumin and calcium and lower CRP than those who initiated with a CVC (all p<0.001). MAP was slightly lower in the AVF group (p=0.047). These differences indicate baseline clinical imbalance and should not be interpreted as effects of access type.

sec.title: Centre variation and the database-recorded centre classification
sec.p: Initial AVF use ranged from 18.9% to 49.0% across hospitals (table 2). A post hoc exploratory grouping based on the centre classification recorded in the source database yielded initial AVF use in 243/559 patients (43.5%) at the two centres in the designated category and 203/662 (30.7%) at the other four centres (unadjusted descriptive p<0.001). The other four centres subsequently developed vascular-access teams, but establishment dates and standardised operational details were not captured. Accordingly, this grouping does not represent a stable comparison of centres with versus without a team, was not treated as an individual-level exposure and was not interpreted as an independent team effect.

sec.title: Clinical and biochemical status at 3 months
sec.p: Available-case descriptive comparisons are shown in table 3. The CVC group had lower median haemoglobin, albumin and calcium and higher CRP. MAP, phosphorus and PTH did not differ at p<0.05. In outcome-specific models adjusted for baseline value, age, sex, diabetic nephropathy and hospital, nominal associations were observed for haemoglobin (adjusted mean difference for AVF vs CVC 2.38 g/L, 95% CI 0.34 to 4.42; p=0.022) and log2 CRP (−0.25, 95% CI −0.50 to −0.01; p=0.044), but neither remained statistically significant after false-discovery-rate control (both q=0.135). No robust adjusted association was identified for any of the seven outcomes (online supplemental table S1).

sec.title: Patient-level factors associated with initial AVF use
sec.p: In the multiply imputed, centre-adjusted model, higher baseline haemoglobin, albumin and calcium and lower CRP were associated with initial AVF use (table 4). Age, sex, insurance, education, diabetic nephropathy and MAP were not independently associated. Hospital fixed effects were used because only six centres were available; the database-recorded centre classification was not estimated simultaneously because it was completely determined by hospital. Complete-case estimates (n=1115) were similar (online supplemental table S2). Variable missingness overall and stratified by vascular access group is presented (online supplemental table S3). All non-intercept variance inflation factors were<1.57. In the complete-case dataset, the model area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.760 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.730 to 0.789), and the Hosmer-Lemeshow test gave χ²=3.15, 8 df, p=0.925.

sec.title: Calendar-year pattern in initial AVF use
sec.p: The proportion initiating with an AVF was 38.5% in 2019, 40.9% in 2020, 42.3% in 2021, 32.2% in 2022 and 31.8% in 2023 (figure 2). This descriptive pattern did not show a sustained increase.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this six-centre cohort, approximately one-third of incident haemodialysis patients started with an AVF. Substantial between-centre variation and marked baseline differences were present. Higher haemoglobin, albumin and calcium and lower CRP were associated with AVF use after adjustment, but the retrospective data cannot distinguish whether these measurements influenced access planning or instead marked earlier referral, better predialysis care, less acute illness or other unmeasured factors.

The AVF proportion is broadly consistent with reports that many incident patients begin haemodialysis with a catheter.11–16 A mature AVF requires advance assessment, creation and maturation; urgent clinical presentation may therefore lead to catheter use. The database-recorded centre grouping differed descriptively in AVF use, but it did not represent a stable contrast in team availability: the other four centres subsequently developed vascular-access teams, and the database did not record establishment dates or standardised operational details. This exploratory finding should generate service-level hypotheses rather than establish an independent or causal team effect.

The higher CRP observed in the CVC group does not establish a catheter-procedure complication. CRP was measured within 1 week before dialysis initiation, but its exact timing relative to catheter insertion and evidence of infection were unavailable. Inflammation may reflect acute illness, uraemia, comorbidity or catheter-related factors. Moreover, the database did not contain longitudinal access patency, access infection, thrombosis or access-revision data, so the relationship between inflammation and AVF or CVC patency could not be evaluated.

CVCs were heterogeneous: 413 were tunnelled cuffed and 362 were non-tunnelled. Tunnelled cuffed catheters may be used for intermediate-term or longer-term treatment, whereas non-tunnelled catheters are generally temporary. Because dwell time and subsequent access changes were not recorded, describing all CVCs as semi-permanent would be inaccurate. The biological processes reviewed by Mima—including endothelial injury, neointimal hyperplasia, thrombosis and inflammation—provide relevant context for AVF dysfunction, but our data cannot test those mechanisms.17

The unadjusted 3-month differences were substantially attenuated after adjustment for the corresponding baseline measurement and centre. None remained statistically robust after false-discovery-rate control. These results are compatible with confounding by indication and baseline severity and do not demonstrate that initial access type changed subsequent laboratory values. They also should not be labelled dialysis quality because Kt/V, urea reduction ratio, delivered dialysis dose and treatment adherence were not available.

Clinical decisions should be individualised. Although AVFs are durable and avoid catheter-related complications for many patients, the 2019 Kidney Disease Outcomes Quality Initiative (KDOQI) guideline emphasises an ESKD Life-Plan rather than a uniform AVF-first rule and recognises that a tunnelled catheter can be appropriate for selected patients.10 Our findings support timely predialysis assessment and planned access discussions, while leaving access selection to patient goals, prognosis, anatomy, urgency and expected treatment trajectory.

Strengths of this study include its multicentre design, 5-year inclusion period, patient-level reanalysis, centre adjustment, multiple imputation, complete-case sensitivity analysis and explicit reporting of outcome-specific denominators. The flow diagram and data audit clarify the analytical cohort and exclusions.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: First, the retrospective observational design is vulnerable to confounding by indication, reverse temporality and residual confounding; referral timing, acute illness, comorbidity burden, cardiovascular status, frailty, medications and predialysis nephrology exposure were not captured. Second, the source database was assembled for clinical rather than research purposes. Some measurements were missing or non-numeric, implausible values were set to missing according to prespecified ranges and CRP measurements below detection limits required substitution. Missingness differed by variable and may not have been at random despite multiple imputation and complete-case sensitivity analyses.

Third, the database-recorded centre classification was available for only six hospitals and did not capture the timing or standardised operational details of vascular-access team development. Because the other four centres subsequently developed teams, the grouping cannot be interpreted as a stable with-versus-without-team exposure; centre fixed effects also precluded simultaneous estimation of any independent classification effect. Fourth, exact CRP timing relative to catheter insertion, infection status, catheter dwell time, access changes, AVF maturation, patency, thrombosis, stenosis, interventions, hospitalisation and mortality were unavailable. We therefore could not test whether inflammation arose from catheter placement or was related to access patency. Fifth, Kt/V, urea reduction ratio, dialysis prescription and other adequacy measures were unavailable, so 3-month variables reflect clinical and biochemical status rather than dialysis quality. Finally, all centres were tertiary hospitals in one Chinese region, limiting generalisability.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Initial AVF use was uncommon and varied across six hospitals. Better baseline haemoglobin, albumin and calcium and lower CRP were associated with AVF use after centre adjustment, but these associations do not establish causation. 3-month differences were not robust after baseline adjustment and multiplicity control. The findings support earlier, individualised predialysis vascular-access planning within an ESKD Life-Plan and identify questions for prospectively designed studies with adequacy, patency, infection and patient-centred outcomes.
